formula: I((math + read)/2) ~ I(students/teachers) + english + lunch + calworks + (1 | county)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented response is score = (math + read)/2, which is no column, so response names math, the formula holds the mean and read is ignored. Read CASchools.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: Stock and Watson (2007) fit lm(score ~ stratio + english + lunch + calworks) (Table 7.1, col. 5, the page's fmc5), stratio = students/teachers, with sandwich standard errors and no grouping. The 420 K-6 and K-8 districts repeat within California counties (county, a factor with many levels), so county is filed as the grouping factor, a cluster the source treats as independent; the random intercept is the reader's proposal. teachers only scales students and is ignored as a denominator; district and school are ids; grades, computer, expenditure and income are not in this model.

Read CigarettesSW.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: 48 continental states in 1985 and 1995. Stock and Watson (2007) fit ivreg(log(packs) ~ log(rprice) + log(rincome) | log(rincome) + rtdiff) on the 1995 cross-section (Eq. 12.15) and the same model in 1985-1995 differences, ivreg(ydiff ~ pricediff + incdiff | incdiff + taxsdiff) (Table 12.1), rprice = price/cpi and rincome = income/population/cpi; no random effect. Panel ruling: state is the grouping factor with a random intercept, the differenced model rendered in levels with a year effect. The instruments tax and taxs stay out, as the formula is not IV. cpi and population only deflate price and income and are ignored.

formula: I(fatal/pop * 10000) ~ beertax + cut(drinkage, breaks = 18:22, include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE) + jail + service + miles + unemp + log(income) + year + (1 | state)
notes: Read Fatalities.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: the lower 48 states, 1982-1988. Stock and Watson (2007) Table 10.1 col. (4) fits plm(frate ~ beertax + drinkagec + jail + service + miles + unemp + log(income), index = c("state", "year"), model = "within", effect = "twoways"), frate = fatal/pop * 10000 the deaths per 10,000 residents and drinkagec = cut(drinkage, breaks = 18:22, include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE); the other columns of the table fit pooled OLS, state or state-and-year fixed effects, no random effect. Panel ruling: state is the grouping factor with a random intercept, year a fixed effect. The response column is the death count fatal, fitted Gaussian as a rate, so family gaussian; pop is the rate's denominator and ignored. The night-time, single-vehicle, age-group and alcohol-involved counts are alternate responses and the age-group populations their denominators, all ignored. drinkage is named once for its cut.

formula: school ~ meducation + I(memployment != "none") + log(income) + log(size) + parity + factor(year) + (1 | state)
notes: RULE GAP: the German federal state is filed as the grouping factor (an area factor with many levels, and school tracking is set per state), although read.md makes a country's few exhaustive regions a design factor. Read GSOEP9402.Rd and WinkelmannBoes2009.Rd: 14-year-old children from the GSOEP waves 1994-2002, one row each. Winkelmann and Boes (2009) Table 6.1 fit polr(school ~ meducation + munemp + log(income) + log(size) + parity + year2) as ordered logit and probit, munemp = memployment != "none" and year2 = factor(year); Table 5.1 fits the multinomial logit on the same terms. No random effect; the state intercept is the reader's proposal. school is the track Hauptschule < Realschule < Gymnasium. year is the wave, fitted fixed; birthyear follows from it (the children are 14) and is ignored.

Read Grunfeld.Rd: on pg = subset(Grunfeld, firm != "American Steel") the page fits plm(invest ~ value + capital, data = pg, model = "random", random.method = "swar") and its Amemiya, Wallace-Hussain and Nerlove variants (Baltagi 2005, Tab. 2.1), a firm random intercept; Kleiber and Zeileis (2008) sec. 3.6 (demo Ch-LinearRegression, chunk plm-RE) fit the same model with random.method = "walhus" on General Electric, General Motors and IBM. The subsets stay in notes: the object holds the eleven firms of Grunfeld (1958), 1935-1954, and the documented fit leaves out American Steel. year is the panel time index. Other versions of the panel: rabe_hesketh grunfeld.dta, stata_grunfeld.

formula: log(violent) ~ law + prisoners + density + income + population + afam + cauc + male + year + (1 | state)
notes: Read Guns.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: 50 states and DC, 1977-1999. Stock and Watson (2007) Empirical Exercise 10.1 fits lm(log(violent) ~ law + prisoners + density + income + population + afam + cauc + male + state + year), state and year fixed effects with sandwich standard errors; no random effect. Panel ruling: state is the grouping factor with a random intercept, year a fixed effect. murder and robbery are alternate responses of the exercise.

formula: log(subs) ~ log(price/citations) + log(2000 - foundingyear) + log(charpp * pages/10^6) + (1 | publisher)
notes: Read Journals.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: economics journals, one row each, subscriptions at US libraries in 2000. Stock and Watson (2007) Table 8.2 col. (2) fits lm(subs ~ citeprice + age + chars, data = log(journals)), citeprice = price/citations, age = 2000 - foundingyear, chars = charpp * pages/10^6, all logged, with HC1 standard errors and no grouping. The journals repeat within publisher (a factor with many publishers, Elsevier, Kluwer and Blackwell among them), filed as the grouping factor, a cluster the source treats as independent; the random intercept is the reader's proposal. subs counts library subscriptions and is fitted Gaussian on the log scale, so family gaussian. citations is the denominator of citeprice and ignored; title is the id; society and field are not in this model.

RULE GAP: the source's model is dynamic, each series regressed on lags of all three, which the registry cannot hold; the contemporaneous revenues and grants stand in. Read Municipalities.Rd: 265 Swedish municipalities, 1979-1987, Greene (2003) Table 18.2 (the page shows only summary()). Dahlberg and Johansson (2000, JAE 15, 401-416) estimate a trivariate dynamic panel model of expenditures, own-source revenues and grants by first-differenced GMM with bootstrapped critical values (abstract: one lag in the expenditures equation, no dynamics in the revenues and grants equations); no random effect. Panel ruling: municipality is the grouping factor with a random intercept. Only the expenditures equation is filed, since revenues and grants as responses would regress on the same three series. year is the panel time index.

formula: log(consumption) ~ log(price) + log(eprice) + log(oprice) + log(lprice) + log(heating) + log(income) + (1 | state)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: the page (NaturalGas.Rd, data from Baltagi 2002) only calls summary(); residential natural gas consumption is the demand a reader would model on its own price, the prices of electricity, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas, heating degree days and income, in logs as the same book models gasoline demand (OECDGas). Panel of 6 US states, 1967-1989; state, the panel unit, gets the random intercept and has more than five levels. statecode duplicates state and year is the time index. consumption is a volume stored as integers, filed continuous.

Read OECDGas.Rd (the page only plots) and Baltagi, Econometrics (Springer Texts in Business and Economics), ch. 12, Empirical Example: the Baltagi and Griffin (1983) gasoline demand equation log(Gas/Car) = a + b1 log(Y/N) + b2 log(PMG/PGDP) + b3 log(Car/N) + u (Eq. 12.40) on 18 OECD countries, 1960-1978, fitted by within (Table 12.1), between (Table 12.2) and one-way random effects (Swamy-Arora, Table 12.3; Wallace-Hussain, Amemiya and IMLE, Table 12.4; Stata xtreg, mle, Table 12.7). gas, income, price and cars hold these logs, so the random-effects model is gas ~ income + price + cars with a country intercept. year is the panel time index. The chapter was read in a later edition (msd.com.ua/?p=107677) than the 2002 one the page cites.

formula: log(wage) ~ weeks + south + smsa + married + experience + I(experience^2) + occupation + industry + union + gender + ethnicity + education + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented model is Hausman-Taylor, a random-effects model estimated by instrumental variables (weeks, south, smsa, married, gender and ethnicity exogenous); the instruments are not representable, so the row is its random-intercept model. Read PSID7682.Rd: 595 PSID individuals, 1976-1982 (Cornwell and Rupert 1988). The page fits plm(log(wage) ~ weeks + south + smsa + married + experience + I(experience^2) + occupation + industry + union + gender + ethnicity + education | weeks + south + smsa + married + gender + ethnicity, model = "ht") (Baltagi and Khanti-Akom 1990, Table I, col. HT) and two variants with other exogenous sets and time dummies (Tables II and III). id indexes the individual; year is the time index. Same panel as stata_psidextract.

Read Parade2005.Rd: annual earnings of people in Parade's 2005 survey What People Earn, with age, gender, state and a celebrity flag the package added; celebrities are oversampled. The page only plots log(earnings) by gender and compares Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients of celebrities and others, no model. The people repeat within US states (a factor with many levels), filed as the grouping factor, a cluster the source treats as independent; the model is the reader's proposal on the log scale the page plots.

RULE GAP: name, the first name on each resume, is filed as the grouping factor: the field experiment reuses each name on many resumes, so the name is a sampled stimulus the rows repeat within, nested in ethnicity and gender; the source treats resumes as independent. Read ResumeNames.Rd: fictitious resumes sent to employment ads in Boston and Chicago in 2001 (Bertrand and Mullainathan 2004), ethnicity assigned at random through the name; the page tabulates call by ethnicity, no model. The fictitious resumes are the experiment's stimuli, not simulated data: call records real call-backs. Ads received several resumes each but the table has no ad id; minimum to industry describe the ad. The model is the reader's proposal.

formula: eval ~ beauty + gender + minority + native + tenure + division + credits + (1 | prof)
notes: Read TeachingRatings.Rd: course evaluations at the University of Texas at Austin, 2000-2002, prof the instructor id. The page reproduces Hamermesh and Parker (2005) Table 3: lm(eval ~ beauty + gender + minority + native + tenure + division + credits, weights = students) with standard errors clustered by prof (vcovCL); no random effect, so the prof intercept renders the documented cluster. students, the number of evaluating students, is the weight the formula leaves out and is ignored; age and allstudents are not in this model.

Read USAirlines.Rd and Greene2003.Rd: six US airlines, 1970-1984 (Greene 2003, Table F7.1). Example 13.1, Table 13.2 fits fm_rfirm <- plm(log(cost) ~ log(output) + log(price) + load, data = usair, model = "random"), a firm random intercept; Table 13.1 and Example 7.2 fit pooled, between and fixed-effects versions (Example 7.2 adds I(log(output)^2)). Row 2 is the two-way random-effects model of the same table. year is the panel time index here. Same data as rabe_hesketh airlines.dta.

formula: log(cost) ~ log(output) + log(price) + load + (1 | firm) + (1 | year)
notes: Read Greene2003.Rd, Table 13.2: fm_rft <- plm(log(cost) ~ log(output) + log(price) + load, data = usair, model = "random", effect = "twoways"), crossed random intercepts for firm and year.

formula: fatalities ~ seatbelt + speed65 + speed70 + alcohol + drinkage + log(income) + age + year + (1 | state)
notes: Read USSeatBelts.Rd: 50 states and DC, 1983-1997 (Cohen and Einav 2003); the page only plots fatalities by state. Model from Stock and Watson's seat-belt empirical exercise (ch. 10; Additional Empirical Exercise 10.1 of the 3rd updated edition): regress the fatality rate on sb_useage (seatbelt), speed65, speed70, ba08 (alcohol), drinkage21 (drinkage), ln(income) and age, then add state and time fixed effects; no random effect. Panel ruling: state is the grouping factor with a random intercept, year a fixed effect. fatalities is per million traffic miles; miles and enforce are not in this model.
